title: Why build your own
hookLine: practices last when they're chosen, fitted and written down; the Buddha tuned Sona's effort like a lute
tomorrow: monks begged a hermit to lead them, then poisoned his wine. who?

lines: SONA'S FEET BLEED ON THE PATH.
cards: New apartment, new plan. Up at five, an hour of sitting, a journal, no phone, every single day. Plans like that tend to last until about Thursday.

Sona's plan was harder. He had been a rich young man, and he became a monk with the Buddha. In a forest called the Cool Wood he practiced walking meditation so fiercely that his feet bled on the path.
And still his mind wasn't free. Alone, he started thinking about going home. The Buddha came to him, and asked him about music.

teach.h: TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE: NO MUSIC.
teach.b: When you lived at home, the Buddha asked, were you good at the lute? Yes, said Sona. When the strings were too tight, did it play in tune?
No. When they were too loose? No.
And when they were neither too tight nor too loose? Then it played well. It's the same with effort, the Buddha said.
Too much tips into restlessness. Too little sinks into laziness.

teach.h: TUNE EFFORT TO THE RIGHT PITCH.
teach.b: Tune your effort to the right pitch. Sona did, and the story says he reached the freedom he'd been straining for. Here's the teaching inside it.

teach.h: THE MIDDLE WAY, EVEN IN EFFORT.
teach.b: The Buddha's path is a middle way, and that includes effort itself, called viriya. Effort isn't measured by how much it hurts. It's measured by whether the string sounds.
And look at how the Buddha taught. He didn't hand Sona a stricter rule. He reached for the one instrument Sona already knew, and tuned the teaching to him.
That's why this new stretch begins here. A practice that lasts is chosen, not assigned. It's fitted to your instrument, your sleep, your job, your body.
And it gets written down, so you can retune it.
Sona's bleeding feet weren't a failure of devotion. They were a string pulled too tight. The work now is to find your own pitch.

how: Buddhist teachers tell Sona's lute to students who push too hard in meditation; practitioners balance effort through walking and sitting meditation rather than forcing either.

games.q: what does “why build your own” mean?
o: the only real practice is one you invent from nothing
practices last when you choose them, fit them and write them down
a practice works best when a teacher assigns every step

games.q: Sona and the lute: tap the pairs.
p: where Sona walked until his feet bled

s: the harder a practice hurts, the more it's working
Sona's bleeding feet didn't free his mind. the Buddha told him to tune his effort, not tighten it.
the Buddha taught Sona with something Sona already knew
he asked about the lute Sona had played at home and fitted the teaching to it.

games.q: a coworker starts a strict routine: no sugar, gym at 5, an hour of reading nightly. two weeks in she's exhausted and says she has no willpower. what fits Sona's story?
o: her string is too tight: tune the effort to what she can keep, then build.
she should tighten it further; real discipline means pushing through.
she should drop routines entirely; set practices never suit anyone.
games.why: the Buddha didn't scold Sona for weakness. too much effort brings restlessness, too little laziness; the string has to be tuned.

practice: Name one thing you'd want a practice of your own to give you. Then name the most likely thing that would stop it, the alarm, the commute, the tired evening.
Last, choose one small plan for when that happens, and decide, quietly, to build.

wordCard.voice: Why build your own: because a practice lasts when it's chosen, fitted like a tuned string, and written down.

orig.note: Pali: energy, effort. In Sona's story it has to be tuned, not maximized.

carryVoice: Your line: my own. Not too tight, not too loose, tuned the way the Buddha tuned Sona. Day 1587, done.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.55 (Sona Sutta: the lute neither too tight nor too loose; balanced energy)
Vinaya, Mahavagga 5.1 (Sona Kolivisa in the Cool Wood, his feet bleeding on the walking path; his thought of returning home)
